turns.prompt_text: What holes do you see in this?
turns.response_html:
While the pipeline is logically decoupled and structurally sound, evaluating it against real-world edge cases, physical handwriting behaviors, and data scaling reveals several structural "holes."

Here is a candid architectural critique of the vulnerabilities within the system, broken down by module.

## Module A: Spatial & Vision Traps

1. The 2D-to-1D Linearity Paradox

  • The Hole: The system has a strict requirement to translate directly into a linearly readable markdown file while simultaneously ensuring no information was lost from the original raw-note image. These two requirements are inherently at war.
  • The Reality: Handwritten notes are rarely linear. They contain 2D spatial layouts: mind maps, margin callouts pointing to specific sentences with drawn arrows, 2x2 comparison grids, and non-linear brainstorming bubbles.
  • The Consequence: Flattening a 2D spatial graph into a top-to-bottom 1D Markdown document permanently destroys spatial relationships. An arrow drawn from a bottom-page summary back up to a top-page premise cannot be natively represented in standard linear Markdown without losing visual meaning.
  • The Patch: You must define a fallback schema for non-linear structures. Use embedded Mermaid.js graph code blocks for mind maps and flowcharts, or rely on custom HTML/Markdown callout syntax to preserve relational context.

2. Boundary Fracture on Diagram Overlaps

  • The Hole: You plan to break the raw image into overlapping sub-images and save diagram crops as standalone PNGs.
  • The Reality: What happens when a bounding box slices directly through the middle of a complex sketch, an extended equation, or a continuous cursive word?
  • The Consequence: If a diagram spans across two sub-images, your hybrid routing system will either save two fragmented, incomplete PNG crops or duplicate the visual asset. Simple string-matching algorithms (like Levenshtein distance) can deduplicate overlapping text, but they cannot stitch together split image files.
  • The Patch: Sub-image bounding boxes must not be generated by arbitrary grid divisions. They must be dynamically generated via visual contour detection—snapping strictly to whitespace boundaries so that discrete sketches and structural blocks are never bisected.

3. Utensil & Technique Hallucination

  • The Hole: The requirement to note handwriting technique and choice of writing utensil lacks an execution target and relies on high-risk visual inference.
  • The Reality: Distinguishing between a 0.5mm graphite pencil, a black ballpoint pen, and a fine-liner marker from a standard compressed phone photograph is notoriously difficult for Vision-Language Models. Furthermore, the schema does not define where this data goes or what consumes it.
  • The Consequence: The VLM will frequently hallucinate utensil types based on lighting variations or image contrast. If this data isn't structured into a strict metadata schema (e.g., YAML frontmatter), it becomes orphaned prose that clutters the Markdown transcription without adding analytical value.
  • The Patch: Move utensil and technique identification to structured document-level YAML frontmatter as optional, low-confidence tags (e.g., utensil_guess: "graphite_pencil"). Do not let the model weave this analysis into the body text.

## Module B: State & Statistical Traps

4. The Timestamp Immutability Flaw (The "Update/Delete" Blind Spot)

  • The Hole: The compilation script checks if a timestamp exists in .word_stats.md to decide if the note has already been accounted for.
  • The Reality: This assumes notes are strictly append-only and immutable. What happens if you fix a transcription typo in a note, re-run Module A with an upgraded VLM, or delete an obsolete note folder entirely?
  • The Consequence: A simple "timestamp exists" boolean check means updated notes will be ignored, leaving stale data in the aggregate statistics. Conversely, if an updated note is forced to re-compile without subtracting its historical counts first, word frequencies will be double-counted. Deleted notes will leave orphaned counts permanently burned into .comp_word_stats.md.
  • The Patch: Replace the simple timestamp check with a Content-Addressable State Ledger. Store a SHA-256 hash of the .md file alongside the compilation timestamp. If the hash changes, the compiler must first subtract the old .word_stats.md counts from the global aggregate before adding the new ones.

5. OCR Noise & Lexical Fragmentation

  • The Hole: Pulling raw word strings into frequency tuples assumes clean, standardized text inputs.
  • The Reality: Handwritten OCR has character error rates (CER). A word written as "system" might be transcribed once as "systen" and once as "system". Furthermore, normal lexical variation means "compute", "computed", and "computing" will be treated as three entirely separate nodes.
  • The Consequence: Your deductive statistics and visualizations will be polluted by OCR typos and un-lemmatized word variations, fragmenting your highest-frequency nodes and flattening your statistical bell curves.
  • The Patch: Introduce an intermediary Normalization Layer in the Module B tagging script. Before generating integer tuples, run the text through a lemmatizer (to reduce words to their base root) and apply a fuzzy-string clustering threshold to merge obvious OCR typos into their closest valid dictionary word.

6. Inverted Index Scaling & File I/O Bloat

  • The Hole: Storing the entire aggregate word list and the inverted backtrace map inside a single .comp_word_stats.md file.
  • The Reality: As your corpus scales to hundreds or thousands of notes, an inverted index mapping every unique word string back to a list of folder names and local counts will grow exponentially in file size.
  • The Consequence: Storing a massive, highly structured data map inside a Markdown file will cause Git repository bloat, massive merge conflicts, and severe I/O slowdowns every time the Python compiler has to read, parse, and rewrite the entire file to add a single note.
  • The Patch: Decouple the storage layer from the presentation layer. Store the raw aggregate statistics and backtrace maps in a local SQLite database (.metadata/stats.db) or a compressed JSON/Parquet file. Use the Python script to render a human-readable summary or dashboard to .comp_word_stats.md, rather than using the Markdown file as the primary data store.

## Summary Checklist for Architecture Refinement

ComponentCurrent VulnerabilityRecommended Structural Fix

Image SlicingBisection of diagrams/sketches across crop lines.Enforce contour-based whitespace snapping for bounding boxes.
State ManagementTimestamp checks fail on file updates/deletions.Implement SHA-256 file hashing with delta addition/subtraction.
Lexical AnalysisRaw word pulls cause typo and inflection bloat.Add a lemmatization and fuzzy OCR-error correction step.
Data ArchitectureMonolithic Markdown inverted index scales poorly.Use SQLite/JSON for raw index storage; render Markdown as a view.

turns.response_html:
Here is a re-architected specification for the Note-Image System. This version transitions the architecture from a simple procedural script into a resilient, local-first data pipeline.

By separating storage from presentation, introducing a content-addressable state ledger, and isolating non-linear visual structures, this redesign resolves the scalability, OCR noise, and spatial data loss vulnerabilities identified previously.

Note-Image System Architecture (v2.0)

A decoupled, multi-stage processing pipeline designed to ingest raw photographs of handwritten notes, extract linear text and visual assets while preserving spatial intent, and compile incremental, lemmatized lexical statistics across a document corpus.

I. Architectural Principles & Definitions

Core Definitions

  • Raw-Note: An uncompressed or standard raster image (PNG/JPG) containing a photograph or scan of a physical note.
  • Note-Folder: A standalone directory named via a randomized hash (./notes/[hash]/) containing the compiled .md document, extracted visual assets, and local statistical frontmatter.
  • State-Ledger: A transactional, local relational storage file (./.metadata/stats.db or .parquet) that acts as the single source of truth for all word counts, file hashes, and inverted backtraces.
  • Metadata-View: Human-readable Markdown reports (.comp_word_stats.md and .comp_deductive_stats.md) dynamically generated from the State-Ledger rather than serving as the database themselves.

II. Module A: Ingestion & Spatial Vision Pipeline

To prevent data loss and stop Vision-Language Models (VLMs) from hallucinating layout structures, ingestion is split into structured pre-processing and targeted transcription stages.

[Raw-Note Image] 
       │
       ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Stage 1: Contour-Aware Layout Segmentation             │
│ (Snap bounding boxes to whitespace; isolate diagrams)  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Stage 2: Topological Graph Sorting & Callout Mapping   │
│ (Sort reading order; map margin arrows to callout tags)│
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Stage 3: Targeted Transcription & Asset Extraction     │
│ (Text -> Markdown Strings | Sketches -> Saved PNGs)    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Stage 4: Synthesis & Frontmatter Assembly              │
│ (Compile linear .md file with YAML metadata header)    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Stage 1: Contour-Aware Layout Segmentation

  • Whitespace Snapping: Instead of applying arbitrary grid divisions, a lightweight object-detection or contour-mapping algorithm isolates discrete semantic blocks (Header, Paragraph, List, Callout, Sketch).
  • Diagram Isolation: Bounding boxes containing drawings, equations, or non-textual diagrams are padded by 5% along whitespace borders to ensure visual assets are never bisected.

Stage 2: Topological Graph Sorting & Callout Mapping

  • Linearization: Bounding coordinates $(x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2)$ are mapped to a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and sorted top-to-bottom, left-to-right within a defined horizontal tolerance.
  • Non-Linear Preservation: Arrows, margin annotations, or non-linear connections detected during segmentation are translated into structured Markdown callouts or Mermaid.js relational blocks rather than being forced into standard paragraphs: 
    > [!NOTE] Margin Annotation (Ref -> Section 2, Para 1)
> Verify this formula against the reference implementation.

Stage 3: Targeted Transcription & Asset Extraction

  • Text Routing: Text-identified bounding boxes are sent to the VLM with a strict system instruction: Output only transcribed text and standard Markdown formatting tags. Do not add conversational filler.
  • Asset Routing: Diagram bounding boxes bypass transcription entirely. They are cropped, compressed, and saved directly to the folder as ./assets/img_[sub_hash].png.
  • Fuzzy Deduplication: Overlapping text boundaries between adjacent sub-images are reconciled using a Levenshtein distance similarity check ($>85%$ threshold) to automatically strip duplicated boundary strings.

Stage 4: Synthesis & Frontmatter Assembly

  • YAML Frontmatter: Low-confidence visual inferences (handwriting style, writing utensil, paper type) are stripped from the document body and isolated within standardized YAML header metadata.
  • Final Assembly: The linear Markdown body is assembled, embedding image references (![Sketch](./assets/img_[sub_hash].png)) at their exact reading-order timestamps.

III. Module B: Lexical Normalization & State Engine

Module B transitions from fragile, file-based string scraping to a structured data pipeline that supports CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) without double-counting words.

1. The Normalization Layer

Before statistical computation begins, raw Markdown text is cleaned to ensure lexical accuracy:

  1. Syntax Stripping: All Markdown syntax (#, *, [], (), image paths, and code block delimiters) is removed via regex formatting filters.
  2. Stop-Word Filtering: Common English stop-words are stripped from the token pool.
  3. Lemmatization & Fuzzy Clustering: Words are reduced to their root lemma (e.g., computing, computed, and computes converge to compute). A fuzzy-string clustering threshold merges minor OCR transcription typos into valid dictionary roots.

2. The Content-Addressable State Ledger

To support updates and deletions, the simple timestamp check is replaced by an ACID-compliant local database (./.metadata/stats.db) leveraging three core tables:

Table NamePrimary ColumnsPurpose
filesfolder_hash, file_sha256, last_updated, statusTracks document versions. If file_sha256 changes, triggers a delta recompilation.
wordsword_id, lemma_string, global_count, doc_countStores the global frequency tuple metrics across the entire note corpus.
backtracesword_id, folder_hash, local_countThe inverted index mapping every word back to specific source note-folders.

3. Incremental Delta Processing

When the compilation script executes:

  • New Note: Add word counts to words and insert mapping rows into backtraces.
  • Updated Note (SHA-256 Mismatch): Query backtraces for the old folder_hash, subtract those historical counts from words, clear the old backtraces, and re-index the updated document.
  • Deleted Note: Remove the folder's entries from backtraces and decrement the corresponding global counts in words.

IV. Module C: Aggregation Views & Deductive Analytics

Module C acts as the presentation layer, querying the State-Ledger to output human-readable Markdown documents and structured visualization payloads.

1. Markdown View Rendering

Rather than using Markdown files to store massive arrays of data, the Python engine queries ./.metadata/stats.db and renders clean, formatted views:

  • ./.metadata/.comp_word_stats.md: A rendered table displaying the top $N$ words by frequency, alongside formatted summaries of their folder backtraces.
  • ./notes/[hash]/.word_stats.md: A local rendered summary showing the top 3 keyword nodes and localized usage percentages for that specific note.

2. Deductive Statistics Engine

The analytics script queries the global frequencies to compute mathematical distributions across the document corpus, saving the results to ./.metadata/.comp_deductive_stats.md. Calculations include:

  • Measures of Central Tendency: Mean ($\mu$), median, and mode word frequencies across all documents.
  • Variance and Dispersion: Standard deviation ($\sigma$) and Z-scores to identify outlier keywords and specialized vocabulary:

$$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \mu)^2}$$

  • Lexical Density: The ratio of unique lemmas to total words per note-folder, tracking information density over time.

3. Visualization Payload Generation

To bridge the backend data with interactive frontend rendering, the script automatically compiles a decoupled JSON payload (./.metadata/.comp_stats.json) structured specifically for visualization environments:

{
  "corpus_metrics": { "total_notes": 42, "unique_lemmas": 1840, "mean_density": 0.42 },
  "top_nodes": [
    { "word": "algorithm", "count": 142, "doc_count": 18, "z_score": 2.45 },
    { "word": "system", "count": 98, "doc_count": 24, "z_score": 1.82 }
  ],
  "backtrace_graph": {
    "algorithm": [ { "folder": "a1b2c3d4", "count": 12 }, { "folder": "e5f6g7h8", "count": 9 } ]
  }
}

This JSON schema natively feeds into p5.js, D3.js, or external charting tools to render interactive node-link diagrams, word frequency bell curves, and visual backtrace graphs without requiring the frontend to parse Markdown syntax.

To solidify the state ledger in Module B without introducing unnecessary project dependencies, would you prefer to implement the storage layer using a lightweight SQLite database (stats.db), or maintain a strictly file-based approach using a structured JSON/Parquet schema?

Technical Specification & Architectural Report

System: Note-Image Processing and Statistical Corpus Pipeline (v2.0)
Classification: System Architecture Formalization & Technical Reference

Executive Summary

The Note-Image Processing and Statistical Corpus Pipeline (v2.0) is an automated, local-first document ingestion and analytics framework. Designed to function as a specialized routing sub-system within a larger image-processing architecture, it transforms unstructured 2D photographs of handwritten notes into decoupled, linearly readable Markdown graphs.

By separating visual comprehension from statistical computation and isolating raw storage from presentation views, this architecture mitigates common multimodal vulnerabilities—such as layout hallucination, spatial context loss, optical character recognition (OCR) noise, and data corruption during file updates. The end-state is a resilient document corpus that dynamically calculates lemmatized word frequencies, tracks multi-document backtraces, and formats deductive analytics for visualization environments.

System Architecture Overview

The system is structured into three distinct, sequentially dependent modules. Each module operates on a strict schema, ensuring that data passes cleanly from visual segmentation to relational storage and finally to analytical presentation.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ MODULE A: Ingestion & Spatial Vision Pipeline                          │
│ Raw-Note Image ──► Contour Segmentation ──► DAG Sorting ──► Transcription│

│ MODULE B: Lexical Normalization & ACID State Engine                    │
│ Markdown Stream ──► Lemmatizer ──► Content-Addressable Ledger (SQLite) │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ MODULE C: Aggregation Views & Deductive Analytics                      │
│ Ledger Queries ──► Dynamic .md Views ──► Statistical Math ──► JSON Viz │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
ModuleCore FunctionPrimary InputPrimary Output
Module AIngestion & Vision PipelineRaw photograph/scan (PNG/JPG)Standalone Note-Folder with .md file, YAML frontmatter, and image assets
Module BLexical Normalization & StateLinearly readable Markdown textACID-compliant state ledger (./.metadata/stats.db)
Module CAggregation & AnalyticsSQL queries from stats.db.comp_word_stats.md, .comp_deductive_stats.md, and .comp_stats.json

Module A: Ingestion & Spatial Vision Pipeline

Module A is responsible for decomposing physical notes into linear digital text without sacrificing the spatial and relational intent of the original writer. To prevent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) from hallucinating layout structure, the ingestion process is divided into four discrete stages.

Stage 1: Contour-Aware Layout Segmentation

  • Whitespace Snapping: Bounding boxes are generated using a lightweight contour-mapping model rather than arbitrary grid slicing. The image is segmented into discrete semantic blocks: Header, Paragraph, List, Callout, and Sketch.
  • Asset Padding: Bounding boxes identified as diagrams, formulas, or non-textual sketches receive an automatic 5% padding expansion along whitespace borders to ensure intricate visual drawings are never bisected by crop lines.

Stage 2: Topological Graph Sorting & Callout Mapping

  • 2D-to-1D Linearization: Spatial coordinates $(x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2)$ are mapped to a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Nodes are sorted top-to-bottom and left-to-right within a strict horizontal tolerance threshold to establish a standardized reading order.
  • Non-Linear Relational Mapping: Physical margin notes, arrows, and non-linear graphical links are extracted as relational metadata. Instead of forcing these into the main text stream, they are formatted as structured callouts that explicitly reference their target sections:

[!NOTE] Relational Annotation (Target: Section 2, Paragraph 1) Author indicates this workflow must be validated against local environment constraints before deployment.

Stage 3: Targeted Transcription & Asset Extraction

  • Text Routing: Text bounding boxes are dispatched to the VLM with strict system instructions to output only raw text and standard Markdown formatting syntax, stripping all conversational filler.
  • Graphical Asset Routing: Sketch bounding boxes bypass transcription entirely. They are cropped, compressed, and stored natively within the document directory as ./assets/img_[sub_hash].png.
  • Boundary Reconciliation: Overlapping textual regions between adjacent sub-images are evaluated using a Levenshtein distance string-matching algorithm. Strings at bounding boundaries exceeding an 85% similarity threshold are automatically pruned to prevent duplicated phrasing.

Stage 4: Synthesis & Frontmatter Assembly

  • Metadata Isolation: Subjective or low-confidence visual inferences—such as handwriting technique, utensil type (e.g., graphite vs. ballpoint), and physical paper characteristics—are isolated within structured YAML frontmatter at the head of the file.
  • Document Compilation: The final Markdown body is assembled, embedding local relative links to extracted sketches (![Sketch Description](./assets/img_[sub_hash].png)) at their exact topological reading-order timestamp.

Module B: Lexical Normalization & ACID State Engine

Module B transitions the system from simple file scraping to a robust relational data pipeline. It ensures that word usage statistics remain accurate across document modifications, additions, and deletions without risk of double-counting or index bloat.

1. The Normalization Layer

Before statistical analysis occurs, raw Markdown text undergoes a multi-step linguistic normalization process:

  1. Syntax Purge: Regular expressions strip out Markdown formatting tokens (#, *, [], (), URLs, code block delimiters, and YAML header blocks).
  2. Stop-Word Filter: Standard linguistic stop-words (e.g., the, and, is, in) are removed to isolate meaningful vocabulary.
  3. Lemmatization & Error Clustering: Words are reduced to their morphological root lemma using an NLP lemmatizer (e.g., computes, computed, and computing converge to compute). A fuzzy-string clustering pass merges minor OCR character-recognition errors into their closest valid dictionary root.

2. Content-Addressable State Ledger

To replace fragile file-timestamp checks, the system implements a relational SQLite database (./.metadata/stats.db) acting as the transactional source of truth.

Table NameSchema FieldsOperational Purpose
filesfolder_hash (TEXT, PK)
file_sha256 (TEXT)
last_updated (INTEGER)
status (TEXT)		Tracks document integrity. Changes to file_sha256 trigger differential delta updates.
wordsword_id (INTEGER, PK)
lemma_string (TEXT, UNIQUE)

doc_count (INTEGER)		Maintains global frequency metrics across the entire note corpus.
backtracesword_id (INTEGER, FK)
folder_hash (TEXT, FK)
local_count (INTEGER)		An inverted index mapping every unique word root back to its specific source folders.

3. Differential Delta Processing Logic

When the compilation engine scans the corpus, it executes atomic database transactions based on file state:

  • Create (New Note): Parses normalized lemmas, increments global_count and doc_count in words, and inserts corresponding rows into backtraces.
  • Update (Modified Note): If a file's file_sha256 hash differs from the ledger, the system queries backtraces for the old folder_hash, subtracts historical counts from words, purges the old backtrace records, and indexes the newly parsed text.
  • Delete (Removed Note): Identifies orphaned folder hashes, removes their associated entries from backtraces, and decrements the corresponding frequencies in words.

Module C: Aggregation Views & Deductive Analytics

Module C functions as the presentation and analytical engine. It queries the transactional ledger to dynamically render human-readable Markdown reports and compute higher-order statistical distributions for visualization tools.

1. Dynamic Markdown View Rendering

Rather than using Markdown files as databases, Module C generates clean, formatted reporting views derived directly from SQL query sets:

  • Global Corpus View (./.metadata/.comp_word_stats.md): A generated overview listing the top $N$ vocabulary nodes by frequency, formatted with their aggregate counts and expandable backtrace lists linking to source note folders.
  • Local Folder View (./notes/[hash]/.word_stats.md): A localized summary generated inside each note folder, displaying the top 3 mathematical keyword nodes, lexical density scores, and timestamp metadata.

2. Deductive Analytics & Mathematical Formulations

The analytical engine processes global frequency distributions to compute parametric statistics, writing the comprehensive report to ./.metadata/.comp_deductive_stats.md.

Measures of Central Tendency

The system evaluates the corpus vocabulary distribution by tracking the Mean ($\mu$), Median, and Mode of word frequencies across all indexed documents:

$$\mu = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i$$

Where $N$ represents the total number of unique lemmatized words in the corpus, and $x_i$ represents the global count of the $i$-th word.

Variance and Standard Deviation

To measure lexical dispersion and identify specialized technical vocabulary versus common terminology, the system calculates the population standard deviation ($\sigma$):

$$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \mu)^2}$$

Keyword Outlier Identification (Z-Score)

To automatically flag highly significant thematic keywords within individual notes, the engine computes the standard score ($Z$) for each lemma:

$$Z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$

Words maintaining a $Z \ge 2.0$ within a specific document are automatically classified as primary thematic nodes for that file.

Document Lexical Density

To track informational compression across the corpus over time, the lexical density ($D$) of each note is calculated as the ratio of unique lemmas ($L_{unique}$) to total words analyzed ($T_{total}$):

$$D = \frac{L_{unique}}{T_{total}}$$

3. Decoupled Visualization Schema

To seamlessly interface with frontend graphing environments (such as p5.js, D3.js, or external business intelligence tools), Module C exports a structured JSON payload (./.metadata/.comp_stats.json). This eliminates the need for visual parsers to scrape syntax from Markdown files.

{
  "metadata": {
    "generated_at": "2026-07-26T18:50:11-05:00",
    "total_notes_indexed": 42,
    "unique_lemmas": 1840,

Because this technical specification includes LaTeX mathematical formulas (for the deductive analytics section), structured ASCII diagrams, and Markdown callout blocks, standard basic Markdown-to-PDF converters will often fail to render the math equations correctly.

Here are the three best methods to compile this report into a presentation-grade, publication-ready PDF, ordered by layout quality and math rendering precision.

Method 1: Pandoc + Typst (The CLI Standard — Recommended)

This is the gold standard for technical documentation. Pandoc natively understands Markdown, LaTeX math equations, and tables, while Typst acts as a blazing-fast, modern PDF rendering engine that produces beautiful typography without the bloated overhead of a full LaTeX installation.

1. Install the Prerequisites

If using macOS (via Homebrew) or Linux:

# macOS
brew install pandoc typst

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt install pandoc
# Download typst binary or install via cargo: cargo install --locked typst-cli

2. Save and Compile

  1. Save the Report Markdown from the previous response as report.md.
  2. Run the following command in your terminal:
pandoc report.md \
  -o Note-Image_System_v2.0_Report.pdf \
  --pdf-engine=typst \
  -V geometry:margin=1in \
  --toc \
  --toc-depth=2
  • Why this works: The --toc flag automatically generates a clean Table of Contents on the title page, while --pdf-engine=typst ensures that your $\mu$, $\sigma$, and Z-score equations render with textbook-quality mathematical typography.

Method 2: Python Build Script (For Integration into Module C)

Since your system architecture already leverages Python for Module B and Module C, you can integrate PDF generation directly into your automated pipeline using markdown, pygments (for code highlighting), and weasyprint.

1. Install Dependencies

pip install markdown pymdown-extensions weasyprint

2. Create the Compiler Script (build_pdf.py)

Save the following script in your project root. It converts the Markdown into HTML (injecting MathJax for LaTeX rendering and custom CSS for professional table/grid styling) and compiles it into a PDF.

import markdown
from weasyprint import HTML, CSS

def compile_report_to_pdf(md_filepath: str, pdf_filepath: str):
    # Read raw Markdown
    with open(md_filepath, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        md_text = f.read()

    # Define Markdown extensions for tables, code blocks, and math
    extensions = [
        "tables",
        "fenced_code",
        "pymdownx.arithmatex",
        "pymdownx.superfences",
        "pymdownx.details",
    ]
    
    extension_configs = {
        "pymdownx.arithmatex": {"generic": True}
    }

    # Convert Markdown to HTML
    html_body = markdown.markdown(
        md_text, 
        extensions=extensions, 
        extension_configs=extension_configs
    )

    # Wrap in a clean HTML document with professional print CSS
    full_html = f"""
    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html>
    <head>
        <meta charset="utf-8">
        <title>Technical Specification</title>
        <script src="https://polyfill.io/v3/polyfill.min.js?features=es6"></script>
        <script id="MathJax-script" async src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js"></script>
        <style>
            @page {{
                size: A4;
                margin: 20mm 20mm 20mm 20mm;
                @bottom-right {{
                    content: counter(page) " / " counter(pages);
                    font-family: 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif;
                    font-size: 9pt;
                    color: #666;
                }}
            }}
            body {{
                font-family: 'Helvetica Neue', Arial, sans-serif;
                color: #222;
                line-height: 1.6;
                font-size: 10.5pt;
            }}
            h1, h2, h3 {{
                color: #111;
                font-weight: 600;
                page-break-after: avoid;
            }}
            h1 {{ font-size: 20pt; border-bottom: 2px solid #222; padding-bottom: 6px; }}
            h2 {{ font-size: 14pt; border-bottom: 1px solid #ddd; padding-bottom: 4px; margin-top: 24px; }}
            h3 {{ font-size: 12pt; margin-top: 18px; }}
            
            /* Table Styling */
            table {{
                width: 100%;
                border-collapse: collapse;
                margin: 16px 0;
                font-size: 9.5pt;
                page-break-inside: avoid;
            }}
            th, td {{
                border: 1px solid #ccc;
                padding: 8px 10px;
                text-align: left;
            }}
            th {{
                background-color: #f4f4f5;
                font-weight: bold;
            }}
            
            /* Code & Blockquote Styling */
            pre, code {{
                font-family: 'Menlo', 'Consolas', monospace;
                background-color: #f8f9fa;
                border-radius: 3px;
            }}
            pre {{
                padding: 12px;
                border: 1px solid #e9ecef;
                white-space: pre-wrap;
                font-size: 8.5pt;
                page-break-inside: avoid;
            }}
            blockquote {{
                border-left: 4px solid #0066cc;
                margin: 16px 0;
                padding: 8px 16px;
                background-color: #f0f7ff;
                color: #333;
            }}
        </style>
    </head>
    <body>
        {html_body}
    </body>
    </html>
    """

    # Compile HTML to PDF using WeasyPrint
    HTML(string=full_html).write_pdf(pdf_filepath)
    print(f"Successfully generated: {pdf_filepath}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    compile_report_to_pdf("report.md", "Note-Image_System_v2.0_Report.pdf")
